title: If one teammate wins, does the whole team win?
answer: Yes. A successful win condition for either teammate wins the game for both teammates.
explanation: Approach of the Second Sun must resolve after being cast from your hand, and you must have cast another spell named Approach of the Second Sun earlier this game. The earlier spell need not have resolved or been cast from your hand. A copy that was not cast does not supply an earlier cast. If the resolving spell meets its condition and no restriction prevents winning, both teammates win.
example: Your Approach of the Second Sun resolves from your hand after you previously cast another spell with that name this game. If its win instruction succeeds, you and your teammate win together.
exceptions: A can’t-win restriction can stop an alternative win. If a player would win and lose simultaneously, CR 104.3f gives the loss precedence.
On a nonwinning resolution, follow Approach’s other instructions. Casting an opponent’s Approach earlier can count for you; your teammate casting one does not count as your cast.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: If one teammate loses, can the other keep playing?
answer: No. Either teammate losing eliminates the whole team, even if the other player has a healthy library and useful permanents.
explanation: No. Either teammate losing eliminates the whole team, even if the other player has a healthy library and useful permanents.
example: Phage enters under your control after you cast her from the command zone, not your hand. If her lose-the-game trigger resolves without protection, both teammates lose.
exceptions: A relevant can’t-lose effect can prevent a loss; concession follows its own rule.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does milling one opponent cause both teammates to lose?
answer: An empty library alone does not cause a loss. When that opponent subsequently attempts an unreplaced draw from the empty library, the loss at the next state-based-action check eliminates their entire team.
explanation: You do not need to mill both opponents. Libraries remain separate. Milling moves cards from a library to its graveyard; having no cards left is not itself a loss. A required draw with no card available causes that player to lose when state-based actions are next checked, eliminating their whole team.
example: Opponent A has 30 cards in their library and opponent B has 70. You mill A for 30. Nothing loses yet. A then attempts an unreplaced draw from the empty library. At the next state-based-action check, A and B lose together; B’s 70 cards do not save the team.
exceptions: A draw replacement or a can’t-lose effect may change the outcome. Milling is not the same action as drawing.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do I lose for drawing the last card in my library?
answer: No. Drawing the last available card succeeds. A later draw attempt with no card available is the problem.
explanation: No. Drawing the last available card succeeds. A later draw attempt with no card available is the problem.
example: Your library contains one card. You draw it in the shared draw step and now have an empty library. That successful draw does not make your team lose.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: What if a draw instruction asks for more cards than remain?
answer: Draw as many cards as are available, one at a time. An unfulfilled draw from the empty library causes a loss at the next state-based-action check, rather than stopping the resolving spell at that moment.
explanation: Draw as many cards as are available, one at a time. An unfulfilled draw from the empty library causes a loss at the next state-based-action check, rather than stopping the resolving spell at that moment.
example: An instruction says draw three cards, but you have two. You draw those two and fail the third draw. Finish resolving that spell or ability; absent a replacement or protection, your team loses before a player next receives priority.
exceptions: If an empty-library draw is replaced by a win, that win can instead end the game immediately.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can my teammate’s library supply a card for my draw?
answer: No. Each player draws from their own library. Sharing a draw step does not combine libraries or let one teammate draw for the other.
explanation: No. Each player draws from their own library. Sharing a draw step does not combine libraries or let one teammate draw for the other.
example: You have no cards in your library and your teammate has 50. During an ordinary team draw step you each draw your own card. Your failed draw still threatens the whole team.
exceptions: An effect that skips or replaces your draw must be applied before assuming a failed draw occurs.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can I respond after a failed draw to avoid losing?
answer: You cannot respond to the state-based loss. Protect yourself, replace the draw, or put a card into the library before the draw instruction resolves.
explanation: You cannot respond to the state-based loss. Protect yourself, replace the draw, or put a card into the library before the draw instruction resolves.
example: A draw spell is on the stack and your library is empty. You may respond with a suitable instant before it resolves. Once it resolves and an unreplaced empty draw occurs, ordinary priority does not provide a rescue window before the loss check.
exceptions: State-based actions wait until the resolving spell or ability finishes. A relevant replacement or effect within that resolution can matter.
Refilling the library after the failed draw does not erase that attempt; the next loss check still sees it.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can Laboratory Maniac or Jace, Wielder of Mysteries win for both teammates?
answer: Yes, if its controller would draw from their own empty library and its replacement effect applies. That individual win becomes a team win.
explanation: Both cards replace their controller’s own empty-library draw with a win. Jace’s static ability is the relevant replacement here, not a permission to use a teammate’s library. The replacement must still apply when that draw would happen.
example: You control Laboratory Maniac, have an empty library, and resolve a draw effect. Its replacement turns your draw into a win for your team. Your teammate having an empty library instead does not satisfy your Maniac.
exceptions: The Maniac must be present when the draw would happen. An opponent can remove it before the draw resolves; can’t-win effects also matter.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: When does a team lose for zero or negative life?
answer: The shared life total being zero or lower causes a loss when state-based actions are checked. There is no separate positive life total for the other teammate.
explanation: The shared life total being zero or lower causes a loss when state-based actions are checked. There is no separate positive life total for the other teammate.
example: Your team has 5 life. An opponent makes one teammate lose 6 life. The shared total becomes −1, and the team loses at the next state-based-action check unless an applicable protection prevents it.
exceptions: A can’t-lose effect may prevent the loss. Life can briefly fall below zero and be restored during one resolving spell before the check.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do damage totals from different commanders combine for a commander-damage loss?
answer: No. Track each commander separately. Different commanders do not combine into one 21-damage total.
explanation: No. Track each commander separately. Different commanders do not combine into one 21-damage total.
example: One opposing commander has dealt you 12 combat damage and the other has dealt you 12. That is 24 damage toward shared life, but neither individual commander has reached 21 against you.
exceptions: A commander can still deal ordinary damage that reduces shared life to zero. Changing that commander’s controller does not reset its accumulated commander damage.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does gaining life erase poison or commander damage?
answer: No. Life gain changes the shared life total, not poison counters or the history of combat damage dealt by a commander.
explanation: No. Life gain changes the shared life total, not poison counters or the history of combat damage dealt by a commander.
example: You have received 20 combat damage from a commander and then your team gains 30 life. One more combat damage from that same commander to you still reaches 21.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can I concede without eliminating my teammate?
answer: No. One teammate conceding makes the team leave immediately. A can’t-lose effect does not force someone to remain in the game.
explanation: No. One teammate conceding makes the team leave immediately. A can’t-lose effect does not force someone to remain in the game.
example: You control Platinum Angel but decide to concede. Your teammate cannot continue the game alone; your entire team leaves and loses.
exceptions: Tournament conduct, penalties and match procedures are administered separately by the organizer or judge.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does a restriction saying I can’t win also restrict my teammate?
answer: Yes. An effect saying a player can’t win also prevents that player’s team from winning through a win effect.
explanation: Yes. An effect saying a player can’t win also prevents that player’s team from winning through a win effect.
example: You control Abyssal Persecutor. Even if your teammate resolves a normally successful Thassa’s Oracle trigger, your team cannot win through that effect while the restriction applies.
exceptions: Concession and all-opponents-leaving rules are separate from trying to resolve an alternative win condition.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does a can’t-lose effect by itself stop an opponent’s alternative win?
answer: No. Preventing your team from losing does not by itself prevent the opposing team from winning. A separate can’t-win restriction is needed.
explanation: No. Preventing your team from losing does not by itself prevent the opposing team from winning. A separate can’t-win restriction is needed.
example: Lich’s Mastery protects your team from losing. An opponent’s successful Thassa’s Oracle win can still end the game because Mastery does not say opponents can’t win.
exceptions: Platinum Angel has both relevant restrictions, so its result differs from a card that only says you can’t lose.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does Angel’s Grace protect my teammate from losing this turn?
answer: Its can’t-lose and opponents-can’t-win clauses protect your team for the turn. Its damage-to-you clause does not automatically protect damage dealt to your teammate.
explanation: Its can’t-lose and opponents-can’t-win clauses protect your team for the turn. Its damage-to-you clause does not automatically protect damage dealt to your teammate.
example: You resolve Angel’s Grace before your teammate’s unpaid Pact trigger resolves. The team is protected from that loss event for the turn. Do not assume the spell also makes all damage to your teammate leave your team at 1 life.
exceptions: Its split second does not counter spells or abilities already on the stack. Detailed teammate-damage calculations remain subject to their own source analysis.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does temporary protection queue every prevented loss for later?
answer: No. A one-time lose-the-game instruction that fails under protection is not automatically repeated later. An ongoing lethal life or poison condition is checked again after protection expires.
explanation: No. A one-time lose-the-game instruction that fails under protection is not automatically repeated later. An ongoing lethal life or poison condition is checked again after protection expires.
example: Angel’s Grace stops an unpaid Pact’s lose-the-game instruction. That specific instruction does not retry next turn. But if your team is still at zero life when Grace expires, the next state-based-action check can make your team lose.
exceptions: Another failed draw after protection ends can create a new loss. Protection is not permission to ignore future required payments.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does one teammate’s unpaid Pact cause a team loss?
answer: Yes. If that player’s Pact payment is not made and its lose instruction succeeds, the entire team loses. The other teammate’s mana pool cannot pay that cost.
explanation: Yes. If that player’s Pact payment is not made and its lose instruction succeeds, the entire team loses. The other teammate’s mana pool cannot pay that cost.
example: Your Pact of Negation upkeep trigger resolves and you cannot pay its required mana. Your teammate has enough untapped lands, but their mana is not yours. Unless a relevant effect prevents the loss, both teammates lose.
exceptions: A specifically applicable mana-granting effect or can’t-lose effect can change the result; merely sharing a turn does not.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Do extra-turn spells also expose the whole team to their delayed loss?
answer: Yes. A granted extra turn is a team turn. If the spell later makes its controller lose and that instruction succeeds, both teammates lose.
explanation: Yes. A granted extra turn is a team turn. If the spell later makes its controller lose and that instruction succeeds, both teammates lose.
example: You resolve Final Fortune. Both teammates take the extra turn. At that turn’s end step its delayed trigger tells you to lose; if it resolves without protection, your entire team loses.
exceptions: Countering or otherwise stopping a delayed trigger is different from removing a permanent. The ability’s actual wording and timing matter.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can “target player loses the game” eliminate a team with 60 life?
answer: Yes. A successful explicit lose-the-game effect on one opponent eliminates that opponent’s team regardless of shared life.
explanation: Yes. A successful explicit lose-the-game effect on one opponent eliminates that opponent’s team regardless of shared life.
example: Door to Nothingness targets one opposing player. If its ability resolves and the loss is not prevented, both opposing teammates lose even at 60 shared life.
exceptions: The ability must have a legal target and can be disrupted. Relevant can’t-lose restrictions still apply.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: What happens if both teams lose at the same time?
answer: If all remaining teams lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
explanation: If all remaining teams lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
example: Both teams have 4 life. Earthquake with X = 2 deals 2 damage to each of the four players, reducing each shared total by 4. If nothing prevents a loss, both teams reach zero together and the next state-based-action check produces a draw.
exceptions: A team protected from losing may survive while the other loses. Separate triggers resolving one after another are not automatically simultaneous.

A can’t-win restriction can also prevent a team from winning through an alternate-win effect. Apply applicable restrictions before deciding that every remaining team actually loses or that a win succeeds.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can a life-gain trigger save us after lethal damage?
answer: A trigger waiting to go on the stack does not resolve before state-based actions. A team already at zero or less usually loses before that trigger can save it.
explanation: A trigger waiting to go on the stack does not resolve before state-based actions. A team already at zero or less usually loses before that trigger can save it.
example: A resolved effect leaves your team at −2 and causes an ability that will gain 5 life to trigger. Without protection, the team loses before that waiting life-gain ability is put on the stack and resolves.
exceptions: Life gained during the same resolving spell or ability can restore a positive total before the check. Gaining life before the damage resolves can also work.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Are all infinite combos automatic draws?
answer: No. A loop containing only mandatory actions can draw the game. An optional repeatable combo does not become a draw merely because a player calls it infinite.
explanation: No. A compulsory loop that cannot be stopped can draw the game under the loop rules. An optional repeatable combo does not become a draw merely because a player calls it infinite.
example: A player can choose whether to activate a repeatable mana ability again. That is an optional loop: propose a finite number of iterations and a resulting game state rather than declaring the game drawn.
exceptions: This FAQ does not add a combo ban, turn restriction or tournament slow-play policy. A judge or organizer may need to supervise a disputed loop.
Players are not forced to spend an unrelated removal spell or take another outside action to break a mandatory loop.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can Brain Freeze followed by a forced draw eliminate one opponent’s whole team?
answer: Yes, if Brain Freeze and its copies empty that opponent’s library, then an unreplaced forced draw makes that same opponent lose. Milling one head and forcing only the other head to draw is not enough.
explanation: Yes, if Brain Freeze and its copies empty that opponent’s library, then an unreplaced forced draw makes that same opponent lose. Milling one head and forcing only the other head to draw is not enough.
example: After enough Brain Freeze copies resolve to mill opponent A’s library empty, resolve Blue Sun’s Zenith with X=1 targeting A. A fails that draw, and A’s entire team loses at the next state-based-action check.
exceptions: This requires enough resolved mill copies and a legal draw target. Graveyard reshuffles, draw replacements, counterspells and can’t-lose effects can change the result.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: What if an effect gives each opposing player a poison counter?
answer: Both opponents receive a counter individually, and their team shares the resulting total. One counter for each opponent adds two poison counters to that team.
explanation: Both opponents receive a counter individually, and their team shares the resulting total. One counter for each opponent adds two poison counters to that team.
example: Prologue to Phyresis resolves against a team with 13 poison. Each opponent gets one: 13 + 1 + 1 = 15. That team loses at the next state-based-action check unless protected.
exceptions: Proliferate has a specific exception: choosing both teammates adds only one poison counter to their team.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: How do infect, toxic and proliferate differ in Two-Headed Giant?
answer: Infect damage to a player produces that many poison counters instead of its usual life loss. Toxic adds its toxic value as poison when the creature deals combat damage to a player, alongside the damage’s other results. Proliferate adds only one poison counter to a chosen poisoned team, even if both heads are chosen.
explanation: Infect damage to a player produces that many poison counters instead of its usual life loss. Toxic adds its toxic value as poison when the creature deals combat damage to a player, alongside the damage’s other results. Proliferate adds only one poison counter to a chosen poisoned team, even if both heads are chosen.
example: An unmodified 3-power infect creature dealing 3 damage adds 3 shared poison instead of losing 3 life. A 3-power creature with toxic 1 and no infect dealing 3 combat damage causes 3 shared life loss and adds 1 poison. Proliferating a team already at 14 poison takes it to 15, not 16.
exceptions: Toxic requires combat damage to a player; infect can apply to noncombat damage too. Prevention and replacement effects can change the results. A team with no poison counter cannot gain its first poison counter from proliferate.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Can teammates combine Gates for Maze’s End or other alternate wins?
answer: No. Maze’s End checks whether its ability controller controls ten or more Gates with different names. Teammates do not pool controlled lands. If one player satisfies the condition and wins, their whole team wins.
explanation: No. Maze’s End checks whether its ability controller controls ten or more Gates with different names. Teammates do not pool controlled lands. If one player satisfies the condition and wins, their whole team wins.
example: You control six differently named Gates and your teammate controls four others. That does not satisfy your Maze’s End. If you alone control ten qualifying Gates when your ability checks, the win can succeed for both teammates.
exceptions: The win check follows the ability’s search and shuffle instructions; the ability need not find a Gate to check your existing Gates. Restrictions that prevent winning still apply.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Does damage to either teammate reduce the same life total?
answer: Yes. Damage is dealt to individual players, and its life-loss result changes the shared total. This does not merge the players or make protection on one head protect the other.
explanation: Yes. Damage is dealt to individual players, and its life-loss result changes the shared total. This does not merge the players or make protection on one head protect the other.
example: Your team is at 60. An opponent deals 4 normal damage to you and 3 to your teammate: 60 − 4 − 3 = 53. Damage to both heads in a single event likewise applies both life-loss results to the one shared pool.
exceptions: Infect, damage prevention, life-total restrictions and replacement effects can alter the normal life-loss result. Commander damage remains tracked separately from shared life.
change_note: New source-verified Winning & Losing FAQ; original summary, not a new Wizards ruling or league policy.

title: Who are “you” and “each opponent”?
answer: “You” normally means the controller of the spell or ability. Your teammate is another player, but is not your opponent. Each opponent means both opposing players.
explanation: “You” normally means the controller of the spell or ability. Your teammate is another player, but is not your opponent. Each opponent means both opposing players.
example: A spell that makes each opponent lose 3 life causes two individual losses of 3: the opposing shared total falls by 6.
exceptions: A reference to your team does not merge control of cards.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What are the life, commander-damage and poison thresholds?
answer: Commander Two-Headed Giant starts at 60 shared life. A team loses at 15 poison. Under CR 903.10a, a player dealt 21 combat damage by the same commander loses, causing their team to lose.
explanation: Commander Two-Headed Giant starts at 60 shared life. A team loses at 15 poison. Under CR 903.10a, a player dealt 21 combat damage by the same commander loses, causing their team to lose.
example: If one head has received 21 combat damage from one commander, their team loses even with life remaining. Yuriko’s life-loss trigger is not commander combat damage.
exceptions: The Wizards format overview uses team-level wording for commander damage; the CR tracks a recipient player. Aggregating damage split between heads is flagged for organizer clarification, not established here as a new league rule.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What does Teferi’s Protection protect?
answer: Its life-total restriction keeps the shared life total from changing. Only its controller gets protection from everything, and only permanents that player controls phase out.
explanation: Its life-total restriction keeps the shared life total from changing. Only its controller gets protection from everything, and only permanents that player controls phase out.
example: Your teammate’s permanents stay on the battlefield. Damage to that teammate can still occur even though the shared life total cannot change.
exceptions: It does not generally prevent poison, commander combat-damage tracking or losing to an empty-library draw. Nonzero life payments cannot be made while the shared total cannot change.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What does Sorin Markov’s −3 do to shared life?
answer: The targeted opponent’s team ends at 10 life if nothing modifies the change. Setting a player’s life total causes that player to gain or lose the difference, adjusting the shared total.
explanation: The targeted opponent’s team ends at 10 life if nothing modifies the change. Setting a player’s life total causes that player to gain or lose the difference, adjusting the shared total.
example: From 60, the targeted head loses 50, so the opposing team goes from 60 to 10. With your Bloodletter active on your turn, that 50 loss becomes 100, taking the team to −40.
exceptions: Life-loss replacements or prohibitions can change the result. Sorin targets an opponent, so it cannot target your teammate.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How do Pox and Bloodletter calculate life loss?
answer: Pox determines each player’s one-third loss from the shared total and rounds each loss up. Both heads lose that amount. Your Bloodletter doubles losses suffered by opponents during your team’s turn.
explanation: Pox determines each player’s one-third loss from the shared total and rounds each loss up. Both heads lose that amount. Your Bloodletter doubles losses suffered by opponents during your team’s turn.
example: At 60 each head loses 20: an unmodified team ends at 20. With your Bloodletter on your turn, each opposing head loses 40: the enemy team ends at −20. Your own team still ends at 20.
exceptions: Pox also discards and sacrifices; follow its whole resolution before state-based actions. Different starting totals and replacement effects change the arithmetic.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Test of Endurance or Felidar win from starting life?
answer: Yes, once their upkeep trigger can resolve with the required shared life total. Test of Endurance checks at least 50; Felidar Sovereign checks at least 40. A player’s win wins the team game.
explanation: Yes, once their upkeep trigger can resolve with the required shared life total. Test of Endurance checks at least 50; Felidar Sovereign checks at least 40. A player’s win wins the team game.
example: At 60 shared life, Test of Endurance can trigger at its controller’s upkeep; falling to 49 before resolution stops that win. Felidar Sovereign instead requires at least 40: beginning upkeep at 40 and remaining at 40 on resolution can win for both teammates.
exceptions: These are intervening-if triggers: meet the threshold both at the start of upkeep and at resolution. A later life-gain trigger cannot create a missed win trigger.
Neither card wins immediately on entering the battlefield. Removing its source after the trigger exists does not by itself stop the ability; a can’t-win restriction still can.
change_note: Reviewed Winning & Losing expansion; append a historical version only if the original seed has no organizer edits.

title: Does one Aetherflux Reservoir activation beat 60 life?
answer: Not by itself. Paying 50 from 60 leaves your team at 10. Dealing 50 to one opposing head takes an unmodified 60-life enemy team to 10.
explanation: Not by itself. Paying 50 from 60 leaves your team at 10. Dealing 50 to one opposing head takes an unmodified 60-life enemy team to 10.
example: From 60 versus 60, one activation leaves both teams at 10. A second activation requires enough life to pay another 50.
exceptions: Only spells Reservoir’s controller casts count toward its cast trigger. Damage prevention, life-gain restrictions and losing at zero can matter.
change_note: Correct classification of the existing negative question: one unmodified 50-damage activation does not beat 60 shared life. Original arithmetic is preserved.

title: Can Rest in Peace and Helm work across teammates?
answer: Yes. Rest in Peace’s graveyard replacement is global. An allied Helm activation with X at least 1 can exile the targeted opponent’s library because no card actually enters that graveyard to meet Helm’s stopping condition.
explanation: Helm repeatedly mills a card until a creature card or X cards have been put into the targeted opponent’s graveyard this way. Rest in Peace replaces those graveyard moves with exile. With X at least 1, the stopping count is never reached, so the remaining library is exiled. Either teammate may control Rest in Peace; the other must control and pay for their Helm.
example: A controls Rest in Peace. B activates B’s Helm with X=1 targeting opponent C. C’s library is exiled. C remains in the game until C fails an unreplaced draw or another loss condition applies; when C loses, C’s teammate loses too.
exceptions: Exiling the library is not itself a win: the opponent must attempt a draw from it, or lose another way. Replacement conflicts, removing Rest in Peace or stopping the activation can break the line.
change_note: Reviewed Winning & Losing expansion; append a historical version only if the original seed has no organizer edits.

title: Does one Platinum Angel protect the whole team from losing?
answer: Yes. Platinum Angel’s “you can’t lose” protects its controller’s whole team from losing. Its “your opponents can’t win” prevents both opposing players, and therefore their team, from winning.
explanation: CR 810.8a applies a player’s can’t-lose and can’t-win restrictions to that player’s entire team. This does not share control of permanents or restore missing resources. Concession still makes the conceding player’s entire team leave the game.
example: Your team can remain in the game at zero life while either teammate controls an active Platinum Angel. An opposing Thassa’s Oracle cannot win through that Angel. If the Angel leaves and your shared life is still zero, your team loses at the next state-based-action check.
exceptions: It does not stop damage, remove poison or restore libraries. Removing or disabling the effect can expose accumulated loss conditions.

Protection from losing does not prevent concession. A failed draw that happened while protected is not permanently remembered after a state-based-action check; later empty draw attempts can still threaten the team.
change_note: Reviewed Winning & Losing expansion; append a historical version only if the original seed has no organizer edits.

title: Do The One Ring or Glacial Chasm shield my teammate?
answer: No. Their controller-specific protection or damage prevention is not shared with the other head. Unlike Teferi’s Protection, these effects do not freeze the shared life total.
explanation: No. Their controller-specific protection or damage prevention is not shared with the other head. Unlike Teferi’s Protection, these effects do not freeze the shared life total.
example: An enemy can attack the unprotected teammate and reduce the shared pool even while you have The One Ring’s protection.
exceptions: Glacial Chasm restricts its controller’s creatures from attacking and requires that player’s cumulative-upkeep life payments; it does not stop an ally’s attacks.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does proliferating both heads add two poison counters?
answer: No. If both teammates are chosen, their team gets only one additional poison counter. The proliferating player chooses which head receives it.
explanation: No. If both teammates are chosen, their team gets only one additional poison counter. The proliferating player chooses which head receives it.
example: An opposing team with 14 poison reaches 15 from a proliferate effect, not 16 by choosing both heads.
exceptions: A team must already have a poison counter for proliferation to add one. Poison dealt separately by sources is a different event.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can my teammate’s empty library enable my Thassa’s Oracle?
answer: No. Oracle checks its controller’s devotion and that controller’s library. Sharing a turn does not share the library.
explanation: Oracle checks the devotion to blue and library of the player controlling its triggered ability, not their teammate’s resources. If X is at least the number of cards in that player’s library when instructed, that player wins and their entire team wins under CR 810.8a.
example: Your library is empty and your teammate has 70 cards. Your Oracle trigger can win for both teammates, even if your devotion is zero at resolution. Your teammate’s empty library instead does not help if your own library is too large.
exceptions: A successful Oracle win wins the whole team game. Check devotion and library size at resolution.
change_note: Reviewed Winning & Losing expansion; append a historical version only if the original seed has no organizer edits.
